subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: What is the full electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16)?
A line emission spectrum shows that electrons in atoms:
choices: Can have any energy at all
Move in straight lines between nuclei
Can only have certain fixed energies
items.note: Discrete lines = transitions between fixed energy levels, each emitting a photon of a specific frequency.

items.stem: The maximum number of electrons in a p sublevel is:
items.note: Three p orbitals × 2 electrons each = 6. s holds 2, d holds 10, f holds 14.

items.stem: What is the electron configuration of Fe²⁺ (Z = 26)?
items.note: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Transition metals lose 4s electrons first when forming ions.
A half-filled 3d sublevel is more stable; Cr and Cu are the two exceptions to learn.

items.stem: Hund's rule states that electrons in orbitals of equal energy:
choices: Pair up in the first orbital before filling the next
Always have opposite spins in separate orbitals
Fill the orbital with the highest energy first
Occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing
items.note: Singly occupied, parallel spins minimise repulsion. The Pauli principle limits each orbital to two electrons with opposite spins.

items.stem: In the hydrogen emission spectrum, lines in the visible region are produced when electrons fall to:
items.note: Transitions to n = 2 (Balmer series) are visible; to n = 1 are UV (Lyman).

items.stem: Lines in a hydrogen emission series get closer together at higher frequency because:
choices: The energy levels converge as n increases
Electrons move more slowly at higher levels
The nucleus attracts outer electrons more strongly
items.note: Energy differences between successive levels decrease, so lines converge to a limit corresponding to ionisation.

items.stem: The convergence limit of the Lyman series is at 3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz. The ionisation energy of hydrogen is about: (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.note: E = hν = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom; × NA = 1.31 × 10⁶ J mol⁻¹ = 1310 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: The first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen because:
choices: Oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen
Oxygen's outer electron is in a new shell
Oxygen has a paired 2p electron that experiences extra repulsion
items.note: N: 2p³ (one in each orbital). O: 2p⁴ has one pair; repulsion makes it easier to remove.

items.stem: Successive ionisation energies of an element (kJ mol⁻¹): 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577, 14 842. The element is in group:
items.note: The big jump is after the 3rd electron, so there are 3 outer (valence) electrons — group 13 (e.g. aluminium).

items.stem: Explain how a line emission spectrum provides evidence for energy levels in atoms.
markscheme: Electrons absorb energy and are excited to higher levels (1)
They fall back to lower levels, emitting photons (1)
Each line has a specific frequency/energy, so only certain energy differences (levels) exist (1)
items.tactic: Link the observation (discrete lines) to the model (fixed levels).

items.stem: Draw the orbital diagram (arrows in boxes) for the 2p sublevel of nitrogen and state the rule it illustrates.
markscheme: Three boxes each with one arrow, all pointing the same way (1)
Hund's rule (electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins first) (1)
items.tactic: Draw boxes for every orbital in the sublevel, even empty ones.

items.stem: Explain the general increase in first ionisation energy across period 3, and the decrease from Mg to Al.
markscheme: Nuclear charge increases across the period (1)
Electrons added to the same shell, so shielding similar; electrons held more strongly (1)
Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital (1)
3p is higher in energy/further from the nucleus and shielded by 3s, so easier to remove (1)
items.tactic: Explain trends with nuclear charge, shielding and distance; exceptions with sublevels.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of an invented element Z: 1st 496, 2nd 4562, 3rd 6910, 4th 9543.
(a) Deduce the group of Z, with a reason. (b) Explain why the second ionisation energy is so much larger than the first. (c) Predict the formula of the chloride of Z.
markscheme: (a) Group 1: large jump after the first electron, so one valence electron (1)
(b) The 2nd electron is removed from a full inner shell (1)
closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so held much more strongly (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
